entities.label: Text
entities.summary:
The Tower of Hercules, located at the entrance of the port of A Coruña in Galicia, Spain, is a lighthouse that dates back to the 1st century CE, specifically constructed during the reign of the Roman Emperor Trajan. It stands as a testament to Roman engineering prowess and maritime navigation, illuminating the Atlantic coast for nearly two millennia. This UNESCO World Heritage Site not only serves as a critical historical landmark but also symbolizes the integration of Roman culture into the Iberian Peninsula, influencing the development of subsequent coastal structures across Europe.

Historically, the Tower of Hercules was built upon the foundations of a prior lighthouse, known as the Farum Brigantium, which served as a navigational aid for ancient mariners. The original tower was likely constructed between 98 and 117 CE, and it is believed to have been designed by the architect Gaius Sevius Lupus. Standing at 55 meters tall, it was the tallest lighthouse of the ancient world, guiding vessels safely into the treacherous waters of the Atlantic. Over centuries, the tower has undergone various renovations, notably in the 18th century, which preserved its functionality and aesthetic appeal.

The legacy of the Tower of Hercules transcends its original purpose as a lighthouse; it has become a symbol of A Coruña and a representation of the enduring influence of Roman architecture in Europe. As maritime navigation evolved, the tower's significance shifted from a practical aid to a cultural icon, inspiring artists, poets, and historians. Its enduring presence reflects the transformation of coastal defenses and navigational aids from antiquity to the modern era, influencing the design of lighthouses worldwide.

'It is the only Roman lighthouse still in use today,' a testament to its remarkable endurance and practical functionality, illustrating the remarkable engineering skills of the Romans and their lasting impact on maritime navigation.
